title: Publish the Web3 & Fintech Developer Academy Cohort Security and Sandbox Testing Playbook, by Fri 11 Dec
description:
Software academies training developers in smart contract security, payments integration, and blockchain engineering face acute cybersecurity risks: malicious contract links, phishing DMs, and insecure testnet credential sharing often compromise student environments. This research and operations playbook establishes strict operational security and sandbox testing protocols for technical fintech cohorts on Zedu.

Work under this goal:
- Map and audit security vectors across cohort discussion channels: handling API keys, testnet faucets, and repository links in public and private channels.
- Build the sandbox testing and security audit channel taxonomy: isolated smart-contract audit rooms (#squad-audit-alpha), security vulnerability disclosure channels, and instructor broadcast alerts.
- Author the vulnerability peer-review and code walkthrough protocol using native Zedu Buzz sessions with screen-sharing safeguards.
- Standardize the testnet credential and test dataset sharing protocols using Zedu File Management with restricted permissions and automatic expiration guidelines.

Done when: A verified fintech academy security standard is published containing channel isolation blueprints, vulnerability review thread templates, credential sharing guidelines, and risk-mitigation checklists verified on zedu-fe.

acceptedWorkstreams.title: Stop fake-admin scams first: staff-only announcements, a verified-staff naming rule and a pinned never-share-keys rule
acceptedWorkstreams.description: In crypto and fintech cohorts the commonest attack is a DM from someone posing as an instructor. Approach, using controls that exist today: set announcement channels to posting restricted so only staff can post there; agree a visible staff naming convention and publish the staff list in a pinned post; pin a rule that staff never ask for keys, seed phrases or payment details by DM; and use testnet-only credentials shared through files rather than chat. List what Zedu doesn't have yet (link scanning, report and block) as gaps. Done: the setup checklist, the pinned texts, and a short incident response for a reported scam DM.

upvotes.reason: "Stop fake-admin scams first: staff-only announcements, a verified-staff naming rule and a pinned never-share-keys rule" is a specific deliverable for this goal with a way to check it was done properly. it fills a gap the goal has open rather than restating what is already covered.
Impersonation DMs are the commonest attack in fintech cohorts; restricting announcements and pinning a staff naming rule uses controls that exist today.
In crypto cohorts the commonest attack is a fake instructor DM; staff-only announcement rights and a naming rule are concrete controls that fit the playbook.
Directly tackles a verified acquisition or conversion friction point with clear, evidence-based scope.

The commonest crypto-cohort attack is a DM impersonating an instructor. Restricting announcements to staff, a visible staff naming rule and a never-share-keys pin use controls that exist today; listing the missing controls is honest.

acceptedWorkstreams.title: Tabletop a leaked testnet key, not only the fake-DM scam
acceptedWorkstreams.description: Prevention is partially covered; response is not. Approach: write and walk through three fictional incidents specific to fintech cohorts - a learner commits a testnet private key to a public repo, a faucet API key is rate-abused, and a demo app session token leaks in a shared screenshot. For each: how the leak is detected, who withdraws or rotates the credential, what evidence is preserved, what the cohort is told and when, and how the leaked material is removed from the channel without repeating it. Keep testnet and mainnet incidents separate. Done: a one-page incident card per case, a rotation checklist, and a disclosure message template. Measured: all three cases reach a named owner and a rotation action in under 30 minutes of tabletop time; no credential appears in the written record; the goal owner signs off. Why it fits: the goal asks for risk-mitigation checklists verified on zedu-fe, and the existing approach covers the fake-admin DM but not what happens after a key is exposed.

upvotes.reason: Simulating high-impact technical failure modes like compromised testnet keys prepares fintech fellows for production security realities beyond social engineering.

This complements the approved prevention checklist by rehearsing what the team does after a credential leak. It uses fictional incidents, keeps testnet separate from mainnet and explicitly forbids recording real secrets; a security owner should verify the rotation steps before the playbook is used.
Directly tackles a verified acquisition or conversion friction point with clear, evidence-based scope.

Correctly splits prevention from response. A committed testnet key, an abused faucet key and a leaked session token in a screenshot are three different detections with three different first moves, and the fictional walkthrough makes each one checkable.

The accepted workstream covers prevention. A key that has already leaked is the case nobody has written down, and fintech cohorts will meet it. Three fictional incidents with detection, rotation and disclosure steps each is the right next piece, and it stays safe because nothing real is used.
